title: Public Value and the BBC
content:
The BBC is under constant pressure to prove its value, and, like many other public institutions, it is viewed through a market-failure lens that limits its role to addressing gaps left by the private sector. It is also measured and evaluated by static, price-focused metrics that fail to capture outcomes that accumulate over time. That pressure is now coming to a head. Before the end of the year, the government will publish its White Paper on the BBC Charter Review, setting out its decisions on how the BBC will be funded, what its mission should be and which public purposes it should serve from 2028. How the BBC’s value is defined and measured will sit at the heart of those decisions.

Subscribe now

The Director-General of the BBC, Matt Brittin has the opportunity to re-shape and re-open the conversation surrounding value creation at the BBC. However, this conversation needs to start in the right way. That requires policymakers and regulators to recognise the BBC’s contribution to the British media landscape.

title: What Does “Public Control” Actually Mean?
content:
“Public control” has become a defining tagline for the new UK government, and a rigorous interpretation of the phrase has the potential to transform the relationship between the public and private sectors in the UK. Andy Burnham used it in Manchester in late June, when he set out a ten-year plan for regions to take greater public control of water, housing, energy and transport. On 20 July, outside Downing Street, he promised to put “life’s essentials back under stronger public control”. At the Labour Party conference in Liverpool at the end of September, he restated the pledge for housing, energy and water and announced a bill to repeal the Thatcher-era ban on public ownership of water companies. Chancellor John Healey has taken up the language too, by promising a “new era of devolution and public control” on arriving at the Treasury, and making public control one of three pillars of his growth speech in Coventry in September. The Budget on 28 October will be the first real test of what public control means in practice.

title: Fiscal Rules Should Serve Britain’s Future
content:
Earlier this month, in his first major speech as the UK’s new Chancellor, John Healey stood in Coventry and reiterated his commitment to “fiscal discipline”. It is not hard to understand why: the UK faces high borrowing costs and weak growth alongside the intense pressure to fund defence, infrastructure and public services. This month, ten-year gilt yields hit their highest level since 2008 and thirty-year yields touched levels not seen since 1998, reflecting changing expectations around medium-term borrowing costs and longer-term fiscal credibility, respectively.

Subscribe now

Much of the rise in gilt yields since the summer reflects a global repricing of long-term debt, not a UK-specific problem, as bond markets reassess debt sustainability and fiscal trajectories across every major advanced economy. Within that broader move, renewed conflict in the Middle East and the resulting oil-price surge are one thread further pushing up expectations around inflation and BoE rate rises, thereby making every pound the UK borrows more expensive.

title: Who Gets to Swim?
content:
During these increasingly hot summer days in London, the issue of who has access to public swimming places could not be more urgent. Since COVID, public pools are no longer what they used to be: a mix of toddlers with parents, pensioners doing their lengths, and edgy teenagers from different socio-economic backgrounds messing about, flirting and screaming. Slowly, they have become quieter and more orderly: adults with pre-booked slots. Small children with parents who had planned the outing days in advance. And almost no teenagers at all.

title: What Carnival Teaches Us About Building The Common Good Economy
content:
This week, Notting Hill Carnival launches its sixtieth year. The carnival happens every year at the end of August and in July celebrates the month to come through a press conference and a launch party, which I am sad to miss due to work I am currently doing in Guatemala and Mexico.

One of the great carnivals of the world, with over two million people filling the streets of West London, is about to make its case. Every year, the coverage tells us the same things: attendance, policing costs, transport disruption, and, if all goes well, the economic boost to London’s hospitality and tourism sector. Those numbers miss the point.

title: What Labour Should Do Next
content:
With the news of Keir Starmer’s resignation, the discussion will turn to who is set to replace him. The inevitable change of leadership also serves an opportune moment to reflect not only on who is best positioned to take the role, but also on the ambition and clarity of vision of Labour’s strategy more broadly.

The mission-oriented framework Starmer set out in 2024 was the right approach to laying out a clear vision for how the British economy could better serve people and planet. However, the government has yet to drive the necessary changes needed to deliver on that vision. As we highlight in our new IIPP report – From Mission Talk to Mission Delivery – the UK’s missions became a slogan rather than a governing architecture.

title: The Common Good Economy: a new compass
content: This morning, after 3 years of writing it, my new book, The Common Good Economy: a new compass, has been published in the UK. It will follow in the US with Basic Venture Group (11 September), and in translation across Europe and beyond: in the Netherlands with Park/Nieuw Amsterdam (25 June), in Germany with Campus (24 September), in Spain with Taurus (27 September), in Italy with Einaudi (October), and in Greece, Poland and Portugal in the coming months. I want to use this Substack to say something about how it came to be, and why I think the argument matters more now than ever.

title: Saving British Steel: Another Bailout or a New Beginning?
content:
As the dust settled after Labour’s devastating election results in Scotland, Wales and England councils last week, Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced on Monday that the government will accelerate plans to nationalise British Steel, identified as a critical ‘sovereign capability’. The steelworks, which employs over 4000 people at its plant in Scunthorpe, is a key piece of Britain’s steel-making capacity, using blast furnaces which allow the metal to be made from scratch rather than relying on scrap. However, the debate around nationalisation overlooks a more critical question: whether the state has the sectoral expertise, long-term financing tools and institutional coherence to govern the steel sector toward transformation rather than survival.

title: ‘Buy British’ isn’t enough
content:
Amidst the US-Israeli war on Iran and ensuing energy crisis, Chancellor Rachel Reeves made two significant announcements last week. Government departments have been instructed, first, to prioritise British suppliers in sectors deemed vital to national security, and second, to ‘insource’ services where possible, with the aim of delivering them publicly rather than contracting private companies. After decades of outsourcing and weak contracts that have infantilised and hollowed out the British public sector, these are important steps. But more must be done to make full strategic use of public budgets to support industrial strategy and inclusive growth, not just short-term defence imperatives.

title: Carnival Economics: Dispatches from Rio, Brasília and Salvador
content:
Last year I wrote about the Notting Hill Carnival in London in an article called Carnival Economics with artist Alvaro Barrington. We argued that conventional economics, and hence policy makers, do not understand the enormous value that carnival creates, not only in terms of the immediate monetary value (receipts of drinks, food etc.) but especially for the sense of community, social cohesion, identity and heritage, skills formation (music, steel drums, costumes, dance, local food) and so much more.

This year we have launched a project on the topic. We are looking at the economic value of carnival, comparing the Notting Hill one with the biggest parties in the world: the Brazil Carnaval!

title: Industrial Strategy: the art of the real deal
content:
Every week there is another horrific story coming out of the United States highlighting the Trump administration’s growing authoritarianism. Within this context, meaningful analysis of his presidency’s economic programme can get lost. With the news of the growing array of companies that the U.S. government is taking equity stakes in, and friends and colleagues weekly asking whether this represents an ‘Entrepreneurial State’ [the title of my 2013 book laying out the myths behind Silicon Valley and the key role of the State in U.S. innovation in the 20th century, I felt compelled to provide a critique of what passes for Industrial Strategy in Trumponomics. The piece explains why Trump, who talks about the ‘art of the deal’, is not providing a good deal for the American public with his policies — and, with at least three years left of his administration, gives some guidance on US industrial strategy done right. Please find the first part of this article below, with the remainder in Foreign Affairs.

title: Closing Out 2025: Don't give up on missions just yet, Prime Minister!
content:
Last week, as we wind down for the Christmas break, Prime Minister Keir Starmer appeared before the Liaison Committee to defend his government's record. One year ago, the Prime Minister launched the government’s Plan for Change, setting milestones for the five missions that Labour had placed at the centre of its agenda. Yet the government appears to have shifted focus from its missions to a narrower emphasis on three priorities that Chancellor Rachel Reeves outlined in November: tackling the cost of living, delivering public services (particularly NHS waiting lists), and reducing national debt. This is misconceived, as I laid out on BBC Radio 4’s Westminster Hour last Sunday. Economic targets like growth, cost of living, and debt reduction are results of investment and innovation at scale—exactly what the missions approach is designed to create, not goals in themselves.

title: Dispatches from Belém
content:
COP30 ended without the fossil fuel phase-out language many had hoped for. Whilst governments of Colombia and the Netherlands stepped forward to announce they will co-host the First International Conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels in April 2026, and 24 countries signed the Belém Declaration supporting a global roadmap, the final COP30 text made no mention of fossil fuels. This was deeply disappointing. Yet what did come through clearly was Brazil’s emphasis on solutions over pledges – and that shift in framing matters. We need to move beyond declarations to the machinery of delivery.

Two weeks ago in a very hot Belém, at Brazil’s “Solutions COP”, we launched two pieces of work that point to what must come next if climate ambition is to become climate action: our State Capacity and Capabilities for a Just Green World report, co-authored with Brazil’s Minister of Management and Innovation in Public Services (MGI), Esther Dweck, and our working paper on Mission-Oriented Country Platforms: Engines for a just green transition. Both have a similar fundamental argument: state capacity is climate policy.

title: Directing Economic Growth: A common good approach
content:
Last week, I had the honour of delivering the 2025 Christian Aid Annual Lecture at St Martin-in-the-Fields Church in London. The lecture, titled “Directing Economic Growth: A common good approach,” explored how we can reimagine our economic systems to serve humanity and the planet: placing the common good at the heart of economic activity rather than treating it as an afterthought. It drew on my work on the Common Good (journal article here), including ideas from a new book I am writing The Common Good Economy: A New Compass—out next Summer.

Christian Aid’s annual lecture series brings together leading thinkers to address pressing global challenges through the lens of justice, dignity and the belief that everyone deserves a good life—now, not later. I was honoured to follow in the footsteps of Amina Mohamed, the former Deputy Secretary-General of the UN, and to speak in a forum dedicated to Christian Aid, an organisation whose mission and history resonates with my own work.

title: School Meals as Moonshots
content:
This autumn is racing to a fast start. In one week, we launched three reports - each trying to push forward our view that the economy CAN be designed to deliver for people and planet if we shape it to be more inclusive and sustainable from the start, instead of picking up the pieces afterwards.

Share

This message is key for progressive governments worldwide that continue to repeat the myth that we must choose either growth or welfare. To me, this is about joining up the Welfare State and what I have coined as the Entrepreneurial State. We can drive innovation to find solutions for societal goals—if we do this right, we get directed growth.

This means adopting a market shaping approach rather than a market fixing one, and as many of you know we have been helping governments to implement these ideas through “mission orientation” at the core of industrial strategies.

Subscribe now

In this Substack, I want to talk about our school meal report as we are launching it this week in Fortaleza, Brazil at the second annual Global Summit of the School Meals Coalition comprised of over 100 countries and patroned by President Lula da Silva.

title: Efficiency at What and for Whom?
content: This piece emerged from conversations at this year's UCL IIPP Forum, "Rethinking the State," where panel after panel returned to the same urgent question: how do we rebuild state capacity in the age of DOGE? We founded the UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose to challenge how the state is imagined, practised, and evaluated—moving beyond the tired narrative of government as bureaucratic burden toward a vision of the entrepreneurial state capable of tackling societal challenges. The Forum title reflects that mission: in an era when democracy itself faces existential threats, we need fundamental rethinking, not incremental reform.

title: From Seville to Belem to Johannesburg
content:
Writing this after an intense (and very hot!) few days at the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development (FfD4) in Seville, one overarching theme emerged from our discussions: the recognition that we don't need more conferences, more ‘blah blah blah’ as Greta Thunberg put it, we need connected joined-up action written into the operating system of our multilateral order.

Share

As Pedro Sánchez, Lula da Silva, and Cyril Ramaphosa wrote in their joint letter at the start of this year, 2025 will be a pivotal year for multilateralism. The three major summits this year—FfD4 in Seville, COP30 in Belém, and the G20 in Johannesburg—offer "a unique opportunity to chart a path toward a more just, inclusive and sustainable world." But only if we treat them as links in a chain, not isolated events.

On Monday, alongside World Bank President Ajay Banga, Spain's Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo, and UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed, we launched a new paper "Mind the Mission, Not the Gap: Rethinking Blended Finance for Public Purpose," co-authored by myself and my UCL IIPP colleague Rogério Vieira de Sá.

title: Giant Footsteps to Follow: remembering Pope Francis’ vision for radically better life on earth
content:
On April 21st 2025, a giant left us. In a world increasingly fractured by nationalism, inequality, and environmental crisis, Pope Francis stood as a potent moral voice calling for a more just and sustainable economic order. His passing leaves an immense void, but also a legacy of hope which must continue to challenge the status quo.

What set Pope Francis apart was his courage to directly connect economic injustice with moral failure—rejecting the notion that markets could be divorced from ethics, and vice-versa. His critique of economic systems that prioritize profit over people catalyzed new conversations about what kind of economy and economics we truly need.

Share

title: The Trump Vacuum
content:
With the madness of Trump's recent tariff announcements and unpredictable policy reversals, the need to demonstrate an alternative vision of global cooperation and leadership is more important than ever. This is what this Substack is about.

With US retreat from global cooperation, we urgently need new global leadership to tackle our greatest shared challenges. The existing economic order was failing even before Trump's return – as evidenced by COP29's minimal progress on climate action and growing inequality worldwide. But Trump's recent announcement of sweeping tariffs and then subsequent sudden retraction has sent shockwaves through the global economy, demonstrating what one might I call the "Trump paradox": even as his administration creates a vacuum in global leadership, his erratic policy moves simultaneously consume an extraordinary amount of global attention and resources. Like a powerful vortex, Trump's economic nationalism both creates a void in international cooperation while hoovering up media coverage, economic analysis, and diplomatic energy that could be directed toward solving our shared challenges.

title: Autumn and Spring Budget Letters: fiscal rules and resisting austerity
content:
Yesterday the UK’s Chancellor of the Exchequer, Rachel Reeves, delivered her Spring Statement to Parliament, signaling a government that is currently stuck between a rock and a hard place. This is partly of the Government’s own making. With such tight fiscal rules, and a refusal to increase taxes, there is an ongoing debate about the degree to which cuts are needed for the government to stick to those rules. In the Autumn, alongside other economists, I argued that for the government to be able to adopt an investment-led strategy, it needed to change those rules. And in another letter to the FT last week, we argued that cuts were not the way to foster growth. These issues are two sides of the same coin. Especially in a country whose real problem is not over-spending but under-investing.
